title: Sterilisation & autoclaves
blurb: How steam sterilisation works, the N, B and S sterilizer types, and how to load, unload and release a load safely.
question: You unload the benchtop sterilizer and the display says 'cycle complete'. One pouch looks scorched and another feels damp. Before anything goes into storage, what must you check, and what happens to those two pouches?

teach.body: HTM 01-05 says saturated steam under pressure is the preferred way to sterilise most dental instruments. Under pressure, steam gets hotter than boiling water and carries a lot of heat, which kills microorganisms, including bacterial spores, when it touches every surface for long enough. The HTM 01-05 figure is 134–138 °C for a minimum of three minutes. The enemy is air: a pocket of trapped air stops steam reaching the metal, so that spot is not sterilised.

items.label: minimum hold time at that temperature
recorded: print-out, data logger or logbook
minimum time to keep cycle records

teach.caption: The three minutes is the holding time at temperature, not the length of the whole cycle.
Types B and N are the ones most often found in dental practices. Use a type S strictly within its manufacturer's list of compatible loads.

teach.h: Why a type N can't do hollow or wrapped loads
teach.body: A type N (non-vacuum) sterilizer removes air passively: steam fills the chamber and pushes the air out. That works for solid instruments sitting in the open. But air trapped inside a narrow lumen, such as a handpiece, or inside a sealed pouch is never pushed out, so steam can't reach it. A type B pulls the air out with a vacuum first, so steam can get into hollow and wrapped loads. That's why HTM 01-05 says only pre-wrap instruments in a vacuum sterilizer.

teach.caption: The door stays locked until the cycle is complete. If any stage fails, the machine shows a fault and the load must not be used.

teach.h: Running the sterilizer day to day
items: Start of day: clean the door seal with a damp non-linting cloth, check the chamber, and fill the reservoir with distilled or RO water.
Run and record the daily tests before any instruments go in.
Load to the manufacturer's instructions. Don't overload: leave space between packs so steam can reach every one.
Before unloading, perform hand hygiene and use clean hands or clean gloves.
Check the print-out or display, the pouches and the indicators before releasing the load, then record the cycle.
End of day: drain, clean and dry the sterilizer and leave it empty with the door open.

root.label: Check the cycle and every pack

children.label: Remove it, repack and reprocess; report scorching

teach.caption: Releasing a load on the basis of its cycle data is called parametric release: every parameter must be met first.

teach.h: A pressure vessel with a logbook
teach.body: Every steam sterilizer is a pressure vessel, covered by the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000. It must have a written scheme of examination and be examined periodically by a Competent Person (Pressure Vessels). It is validated by a Competent Person (Decontamination) or service engineer to prove it reaches the right temperature, pressure and time. Each sterilizer has a logbook recording maintenance, validation, faults, modifications and routine tests.

teach.text: Never put wrapped instruments in a type N sterilizer. With no vacuum, air stays trapped in the pouch and the instruments inside are not sterilised. Type N instruments are wrapped afterwards, aseptically, straight out of the chamber.

items: Steam under pressure: 134–138 °C for a minimum of 3 minutes (HTM 01-05).
Type N: solid, unwrapped only. Type B: vacuum, for hollow and wrapped loads. Type S: the manufacturer's specified loads.
Don't overload: leave space so steam reaches every pack.
Check cycle data, seals and dryness before release. Failed cycle: reprocess the whole load.
Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000: written scheme, Competent Person examination, logbook.

summary: You can now explain how steam sterilisation works and why air must be removed, state the HTM 01-05 temperature and hold time, match loads to type N, B and S sterilizers, run the machine safely through the day, and decide whether a load can be released.

A.q: According to HTM 01-05, which conditions are used for steam sterilisation of dental instruments?
A.why: HTM 01-05 describes steam sterilisation at 134–138 °C for a minimum of three minutes.

whyNot.0: 121 °C cycles need far longer holds and are not the HTM 01-05 figure.
whyNot.3: 80 °C for 10 minutes is a washer-disinfector thermal disinfection setting, not sterilisation.

A.q: A practice wants to sterilise wrapped instruments and handpieces. Which type of sterilizer is suitable?
options: Any type, on a longer cycle
An ultrasonic cleaner with a lid
A.why: Type B sterilizers have a vacuum stage designed for hollow, air-retentive and packaged loads.

whyNot.0: Type N is designed for non-wrapped solid instruments only.
whyNot.2: A longer cycle can't remove air trapped in hollow or wrapped loads.
whyNot.3: Ultrasonic cleaners clean; they don't sterilise.

A.q: A load print-out shows the cycle was interrupted before it finished. What should happen to the instruments?
options: Use them, as they reached temperature
Use only the ones on the top shelf
Wipe them with disinfectant and use them
A.why: Instruments from an unsuccessful or interrupted cycle must not be used; the whole load is reprocessed.

whyNot.0: Reaching temperature briefly doesn't mean the full hold time was achieved.
whyNot.1: No part of a failed load can be assumed sterile.
whyNot.2: Wiping is not sterilisation and doesn't make a failed load safe.

B.q: A benchtop sterilizer is being loaded with pouched instruments. Which practice best supports steam penetration?
options: Packing the trays as tightly as possible
Stacking pouches on top of each other
Wrapping each pouch in a second towel
B.why: Space between packs lets steam circulate and reach every surface. Overloading is a common cause of sterilisation failure.

whyNot.1: Tight packing blocks steam from reaching every pack.
whyNot.2: Stacking traps air and blocks steam contact.
whyNot.3: Extra towels add barriers that steam has to get through and aren't validated packaging.

B.q: Why should wrapped instruments NOT be processed in a type N sterilizer?
options: The pouches would melt in the chamber
Air stays trapped without a vacuum
Type N cycles are too short for pouches
B.why: Type N relies on steam passively pushing air out. Air inside a pouch isn't removed, so steam can't reach the instruments.

whyNot.0: Type N machines do reach sterilising temperature; air removal is the problem.
whyNot.1: Validated pouches don't melt; they just don't let air out in a non-vacuum cycle.
whyNot.3: Cycle length isn't the issue; trapped air is.

B.q: A pouch comes out of the sterilizer scorched. What is the best action?
options: Use it, as the heat proves it is sterile
Remove it from use and report it
Store it at the back of the cupboard
B.why: A scorched pouch suggests a fault and may have damaged packaging. Remove it, reprocess the contents and report it so the cause can be checked.

whyNot.0: Scorching suggests a fault, not proof of sterility.
whyNot.2: Re-labelling hides the problem and doesn't make the pack safe.
whyNot.3: Storing it means it could still be used on a patient.

C.q: Which legislation requires a benchtop sterilizer to have a written scheme of examination?
C.why: Steam sterilizers are pressure vessels, covered by the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000, and must be examined periodically by a Competent Person.

whyNot.0: IRR17 covers radiation, such as dental X-ray equipment.
whyNot.1: COSHH covers hazardous substances, not pressure vessels.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers reporting injuries, diseases and dangerous occurrences.

C.q: You are about to unload a completed cycle. What should you do before handling the packs?
options: Put on the gloves you used for cleaning
Open one pouch to check the contents
Perform hand hygiene and use clean gloves
C.why: Clean hands or clean gloves protect the sterilised packs from recontamination as they are unloaded.

whyNot.0: Gloves used for dirty work would contaminate the clean packs.
whyNot.1: Spraying packs wets them and compromises the barrier.
whyNot.2: Opening a pouch breaks the sterile barrier.

C.q: Which daily task should be done at the end of the working day?
options: Drain, clean and dry it, leaving the door open
Refill the reservoir with tap water for tomorrow
Leave a full load in the chamber overnight
Close the door tightly to keep dust out
C.why: HTM 01-05 says at the end of the day the sterilizer should be cleaned, dried and left empty with the door open.

whyNot.1: Only distilled or RO water is used, and the reservoir is left empty overnight.
whyNot.2: Instruments are never left in the chamber overnight.
whyNot.3: The door is left open so the chamber dries out.

reteach.title: Think of a steam room and a sleeping bag
reteach.question: If you climbed into a hot steam room inside a zipped-up sleeping bag, would the steam reach you? What does that have to do with sterilizer types?

blocks.body: In a steam room you feel the heat because steam touches your skin. Zip yourself into a sleeping bag full of air and the steam can't get in. A pouch or a hollow handpiece is like that sleeping bag. A type N sterilizer just fills the room with steam and hopes the air leaves, which works for bare, solid instruments. A type B first sucks the air out with a vacuum, so the steam can get into the 'sleeping bag'. Then it must hold 134–138 °C for at least 3 minutes.

blocks.text: 'Cycle complete' on the screen is not the end of your checks. You still check the print-out or display values, and that every pack is dry, sealed and undamaged, before it is released.

explain.body: HTM 01-05: steam at 134–138 °C for a minimum of three minutes. The three minutes is the holding time, and air must be removed so steam touches every surface.

test.q: What is the minimum holding time at 134–138 °C stated in HTM 01-05?
test.why: HTM 01-05 states 134–138 °C for a minimum of three minutes.

whyNot.0: One minute is too short at this temperature.
whyNot.2: Ten minutes is linked to thermal disinfection at 80 °C in a washer-disinfector.
whyNot.3: Fifteen minutes is associated with lower-temperature cycles, not the HTM 01-05 figure.

explain.body: Non-vacuum. Steam passively displaces air, so it is only for solid, unwrapped instruments. Instruments are wrapped aseptically after the cycle if they will be stored.

test.q: Which load is suitable for a type N sterilizer?
test.why: Type N sterilizers are designed for non-wrapped solid instruments only.

whyNot.0: Pouches trap air that a type N cannot remove.
whyNot.2: Lumens trap air, so they need a vacuum sterilizer.
whyNot.3: Wrapped kits need a vacuum (type B or S) cycle.

explain.body: Type B has a vacuum stage for hollow, air-retentive and packaged loads. Type S is designed for specific loads that its manufacturer defines, and must be used strictly within those instructions.

test.q: What defines which loads a type S sterilizer can process?
test.why: Type S sterilizers are designed for specific load types; the manufacturer defines exactly which loads or instruments are compatible.

whyNot.0: A local risk assessment can't extend a machine beyond its validated loads.
whyNot.1: Preference doesn't change what the machine is validated for.
whyNot.3: Waste contractors have nothing to do with sterilizer loads.

explain.body: Check the cycle reached its parameters, then check every pack is dry, sealed and undamaged. Failed or interrupted cycle: reprocess the whole load. Scorched, wet or torn pouch: remove and reprocess.

test.q: The display shows the required temperature and hold time were achieved. What should you check next?
options: Pouch seals and the cycle record
The date of the last annual service
The water hardness in the area
test.why: Before release, check each pouch is intact, sealed and dry and that the cycle record confirms the parameters.

whyNot.1: Service dates are checked through the logbook, not at every unload.
whyNot.2: Water hardness isn't a release check.
whyNot.3: Patient arrival has nothing to do with releasing a load.
